title: Palindrome Number
description: Brute force to optimized: string comparison, full arithmetic reversal, then reversing only half the digits.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Problem Summary: Given an integer, determine whether it reads the same forwards and backwards, ideally without converting it to a string.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Detail"],"rows":[["Problem Summary","Given num, decide whether it is a palindrome, meaning it reads the same forwards and backwards."],["Input","num, an integer."],["Output","A boolean: true if num is a palindrome, false otherwise."],["Constraints","-2^31 <= num <= 2^31 minus 1, the typical 32 bit signed integer range for this problem."],["Requirements","There is no array or list to mutate in place, num is a single integer. There is no sequence of outputs whose order needs to stay stable either, the answer is one boolean."]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Detail"],"rows":[["Pattern","Mirror comparison from both ends inward, done either with two pointers on a string or purely with arithmetic directly on the number."],["Difficulty","Beginner"],["Tags","Math"],["Interview Focus","Recognizing negative numbers and trailing-zero numbers (other than 0) can never be palindromes, avoiding string conversion via arithmetic reversal, and recognizing only half the digits ever need reversing."]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given an integer num, decide whether it reads the same forwards and backwards, like 121 or 7, without converting it to a string if possible.

blocks.title: Analogy: Reading a Number in a Mirror
blocks.text: Picture holding a number up to a mirror. If the reflection looks exactly the same as the original, digit for digit, the number is a palindrome. 121 reflected still reads 121. 123 reflected reads 321, clearly different from the original, so it fails the mirror test.

blocks.caption: Comparing digits from the outside in

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: num = 121

blocks.content: {"headers":["Position pair","Digits","Match?","Why"],"rows":[["Outer pair","1 and 1","Yes","The first and last digit are compared first, moving inward from both ends."],["Middle","2","Nothing to compare, single middle digit","With an odd number of digits, the exact middle digit never needs a partner to match against."]]}

blocks.text: Every pair of digits from the outside in matches, so 121 is a palindrome.
Example: num = 123

blocks.content: {"headers":["Position pair","Digits","Match?","Why"],"rows":[["Outer pair","1 and 3","No","The very first comparison from both ends already fails to match."]]}

blocks.text: The very first comparison already fails, so 123 is not a palindrome.
Example: num = -121
Negative numbers are never palindromes, because the minus sign only appears on one side. Reading -121 backwards would give 121-, which is not a valid number at all, so this is rejected immediately.
5. How Should We Think?
Before writing any code, it helps to reason about what a palindrome check really needs.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A palindrome is defined entirely by comparing digits from the outside in, the first digit against the last, the second against the second to last, and so on.

Observation 2: A negative number can never satisfy this, since the minus sign only ever appears on one side, breaking the mirror immediately.

Observation 3: This outside-in comparison can be done on a string with two pointers, but it can also be done purely with arithmetic, peeling digits off one end with modulo and division and rebuilding them in reverse order.

Observation 4: Once a full reversed number can be built with arithmetic, comparing only half of the digits, instead of the entire number, is enough, since a correct second half automatically confirms the first half matches too.
That reasoning alone already sketches the whole path: skip the string, reverse with arithmetic, then realize only half the digits ever need reversing.
6. Brute Force Solution
The most direct approach is to convert the number into a string and compare characters from both ends moving inward, exactly like the mirror analogy describes.
Step by step algorithm

items: If num is negative, return false immediately.
Convert num to a string.
Place one pointer at the start and one at the end.
While the pointers have not crossed, compare the characters they point to.
If any pair does not match, return false. If the pointers meet, return true.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: two pointers closing in from both ends of the string

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The num < 0 check happens before any string conversion, since comparing characters on a negative number's string would otherwise need extra special casing just for the minus sign.
Two pointers start at opposite ends of the string and move toward each other, stopping the instant they cross, so no character pair is ever compared twice.

The loop returns false the moment any single mismatch is found, rather than checking every pair and combining the results afterward, since one mismatch is already enough to disprove the palindrome property.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
This works because a palindrome is defined exactly by this property, every digit from the front must match its mirrored position from the back.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(d), where d is the number of digits, since each pointer moves at most halfway across.
Space: O(d), for the string created to hold the digits.

Limitation: converting to a string allocates extra memory just to get indexable characters. The same comparison can be done directly on the number itself using arithmetic, with no string ever created.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the string based comparison works but is not necessary: converting to a string only exists to get indexable characters, the same digit by digit access is available directly through arithmetic.

What the string allocation costs: O(d) extra space just to hold characters that arithmetic could extract without ever storing them.

Can the digits be extracted without a string: yes, modulo 10 reads the last digit and integer division removes it, repeatable to peel off every digit from the end.

Can a full reversed number be built purely from those extracted digits: yes, multiplying the running reversed value by 10 and adding each new digit rebuilds the number in reverse order.

The core idea: build the number's reverse with pure arithmetic, then compare it to the original, no string ever created.
A number and its mathematical reverse can be compared directly: peel digits off the end of num using modulo 10, and rebuild them in reverse order using ordinary arithmetic, no string needed anywhere.
The optimization is to construct the reversed number as an integer, and compare it against the original.
9. Optimized Solution

Keep a copy of the original number. Repeatedly take the last digit of num with modulo 10, append it to a running reversed number, and remove that digit from num with integer division. Compare the final reversed number to the original.
Dry run for num = 121

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","num","reversedNum","Why"],"rows":[["Start","121","0","The starting values before any digit has been peeled off."],["1","12","1","The last digit, 1, is peeled off num and appended to reversedNum."],["2","1","12","The next digit, 2, is peeled off and appended after the previous one."],["3","0","121","The final digit, 1, is peeled off, num reaches 0 and the loop stops."]]}

blocks.text: The loop stops once num reaches 0. reversedNum ends at 121, equal to the original, confirming it is a palindrome.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: build the full reverse with arithmetic, then compare

blocks.text: Why This Works

This works because a number is a palindrome exactly when it is identical to its own digit-reversed version, and the loop constructs that reversed version directly through arithmetic: each iteration peels the current last digit off num and appends it to the growing reversedNum, which is mathematically equivalent to writing the digits down in reverse order. Comparing the final reversedNum to the untouched original is a direct test of the palindrome definition itself, no string or indexing needed.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["num equals its own digit-reversed value","The loop's reversedNum ends up identical to the saved original","True, palindrome"],["num does not equal its own digit-reversed value","The loop's reversedNum differs from the saved original in at least one digit","False, not a palindrome"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: original is saved before the loop begins specifically because num itself gets consumed, divided down to 0, during the loop, so the untouched starting value has to be kept elsewhere to compare against at the end.

reversedNum is declared as a wider integer type in Java and C++ specifically because reversing certain valid 32 bit inputs can temporarily exceed the range of a normal int before the final comparison even happens.
The loop condition is num > 0, which naturally stops once every digit has been peeled off, without needing to know in advance how many digits num has.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(d), one pass over the digits, the same order as before.
Space: O(1), no string allocated, just a couple of integers.
10. Further Optimization: Reverse Only Half

The optimized solution reverses the entire number before comparing, but only half of it actually needs to be reversed. Once the reversed portion becomes at least as large as what remains of the original, the halfway point has been reached.

Intuition: stop peeling digits off the original as soon as the reversed half catches up to (or passes) what is left of the original, then compare the two halves directly, dropping the middle digit if the total digit count is odd.
Dry run for num = 121

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","num before","num after","revertedHalf","Why"],"rows":[["1","121","12","1","The last digit is peeled off and moved into revertedHalf, num is still larger, so the loop continues."],["2","12","1","12","num (1) is no longer greater than revertedHalf (12), the loop stops right here."]]}

blocks.text: After step 2, num (1) is no longer greater than revertedHalf (12), so the loop stops. Since 121 has an odd number of digits, the extra middle digit sits in revertedHalf, so the comparison drops it: num equals revertedHalf divided by 10, which is 1 equals 1. They match, confirming a palindrome.

blocks.caption: Further optimization: only reverse the second half, then compare halves

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: The early rejection for a number ending in 0 (other than 0 itself) exists because a valid palindrome can never end in a 0 digit unless the whole number is 0, since that would require a leading zero on the other end, which is not how integers are written.

The loop condition num > revertedHalf is what determines the natural stopping point: once the reversed half becomes at least as large as what remains of the original, exactly half, or just over half for odd digit counts, has been processed.

Comparing against both revertedHalf and revertedHalf divided by 10 handles both digit-count cases in one expression: an even total needs an exact match, an odd total needs the middle digit of revertedHalf dropped first.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(d), but only walks roughly half the digits instead of all of them, a real constant factor improvement.
Space: O(1), and additionally avoids the overflow risk of building a full reversed number for very large inputs, since only half the digits are ever reversed.
11. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Solution","Time","Space","Stable Order","Interview Recommendation"],"rows":[["Brute force (string, two pointers)","O(d)","O(d)","Not applicable, single boolean output","Simple and correct, but converting to a string is the first thing worth optimizing away."],["Optimized (full arithmetic reversal)","O(d)","O(1)","Not applicable, single boolean output","Good default answer, removes the string entirely, though it briefly needs a wider integer type to avoid overflow."],["Further optimized (reverse only half)","O(d), roughly half the work","O(1)","Not applicable, single boolean output","Strongest answer, avoids overflow entirely by never fully reversing the number."]]}

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

The core pattern here is mirroring from both ends inward, whether on a string with two pointers or directly on the digits with arithmetic. Recognizing that only half of the digits ever need to be touched is the key insight that separates the fully optimized solution from the merely correct one.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting that negative numbers can never be palindromes.
Reversing the entire number with plain int arithmetic and silently overflowing on very large inputs, when using half reversal or a wider integer type avoids this.
Mishandling numbers that end in 0 (other than 0 itself), which can never be palindromes since a palindrome cannot start with 0.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["Single digit numbers (0 through 9)","Always palindromes, since there is nothing to mismatch against; the comparison loop simply never runs."],["Numbers ending in 0 but not equal to 0 (like 10 or 100)","Can never be palindromes, since a matching leading 0 on the other end is not a valid way to write an integer."],["Very large numbers","Full reversal risks overflow past a 32 bit range; the half reversal approach avoids this risk entirely by never building the full reverse."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips

This problem is often used to test whether a candidate defaults to string conversion or can work with the number directly using arithmetic. Going one step further, only reversing half the digits, shows attention to both performance and correctness details like overflow.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid converting to a string", think: reverse the number with modulo and integer division instead.
If the interviewer says "what about overflow", think: only reverse half the digits instead of the whole number.
If the interviewer says "can you do this in O(1) extra space", think: either arithmetic reversal approach already avoids the string entirely.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Can you solve this without ever converting the number to a string?
Why can a full arithmetic reversal risk overflow, and how does reversing only half the digits avoid that risk?
How would you handle a number so large it does not fit in a normal integer type at all, say given as a string?
Why must a number ending in 0 (other than 0 itself) always fail the palindrome check?
Can you adapt this same half reversal idea to check if a string or linked list is a palindrome?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Any palindrome check, on strings, linked lists, or arrays, which uses the exact same two-pointers-from-both-ends-inward idea.
Digit manipulation problems in general, where peeling digits with modulo and integer division replaces a string conversion.
Overflow aware arithmetic, where reversing only part of a number, or using a wider intermediate type, avoids risking the limits of a fixed size integer type.
Symmetry detection problems more broadly, where a structure only needs to be checked halfway before its own symmetry guarantees the rest.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The string based two pointer approach runs in O(d) time and O(d) space. The full arithmetic reversal runs in O(d) time and O(1) space. Reversing only half the digits keeps O(d) time but touches roughly half as many digits and avoids overflow risk entirely, the strongest version of the three.
13. Final Summary

items: Pattern: mirror comparison from both ends inward, expressed either as two string pointers or as pure digit arithmetic.

Core Idea: a number is a palindrome exactly when it equals its own digit-reversed value, and that reversal can be built with modulo and division alone, without ever creating a string, and only half the digits ever need reversing.
Time: O(d) for every version shown here, where d is the number of digits.
Space: O(d) for the string based version, O(1) for both arithmetic versions.
Most Important Observation: once the second half of a number is confirmed to mirror the first half, the full number is automatically confirmed too, there is never a need to reverse the entire thing.
Interview Difficulty: easy to solve with a string, but avoiding the string and then avoiding overflow are the two follow ups that separate a strong answer.
One line memory trick: build the reverse, or just half of it, with modulo and division, then compare.
